summary: Extends the RFC 1521 message format so that non-ASCII text can appear in email headers, such as in subject lines. It was designed to work with existing mail software. It was replaced by RFC 2045, RFC 2046, RFC 2047, RFC 2048, RFC 2049.

plainLanguage.summary: Older mail programs get confused by unusual text in the header lines of an email, such as a subject written in Greek. This RFC puts that text into a shape those programs pass through untouched, and tells newer programs how to unpack it again for display.

questions: how to put non-ascii text in email headers
what is the difference between q and b encoding
how long can an encoded-word be
subtitle: How non-ASCII text is written into email headers so that old and new mail programs both cope.

tldr.problem: Mail headers were defined to hold only ASCII text, so a subject line or display name in another language had no standard way to travel.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the encoded-word, a run of printable ASCII between the characters =? and ?= that names a character set and an encoding and carries the text in one of two encodings, B and Q.
tldr.outcome: The scheme was designed to survive mail programs that rearrange or rewrite headers. This RFC was later obsoleted by RFC 2045, RFC 2046, RFC 2047, RFC 2048 and RFC 2049.

facts.label: Names
facts.value: Charset and encoding names are case independent

today: RFC 1522 is a Draft Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 2045, RFC 2046, RFC 2047, RFC 2048 and RFC 2049, so read those for the current rules.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1521 describes a mechanism for denoting textual body parts that are coded in various character sets, and methods for encoding such body parts as sequences of printable ASCII characters. This memo describes similar techniques to allow the encoding of non-ASCII text in various portions of an RFC 822 message header, in a manner that is unlikely to confuse existing message handling software.

Some mail relaying programs are known to delete some message header fields while retaining others, rearrange the order of addresses in To or Cc fields, rearrange the vertical order of header fields, or wrap message headers at different places than those in the original message. Some mail reading programs have difficulty parsing headers that make use of backslash-quoting to hide special characters such as <, , or :, or that exploit other infrequently-used features of RFC 822. Breaking these programs would cause severe operational problems for the Internet mail system, so the extensions described here do not rely on little-used features of RFC 822.

Instead, certain sequences of ordinary printable ASCII characters, known as encoded-words, are reserved for use as encoded data, and their syntax is such that they are unlikely to accidentally appear as normal text in message headers. A mail composer that implements this specification provides a means of inputting non-ASCII text in header fields and translates those fields into encoded-words before inserting them into the header. A mail reader recognises encoded-words when they appear in certain portions of the header and, instead of displaying them as they are, reverses the encoding and displays the original text in the designated character set.
sections.plainLanguage: Older mail programs get confused by unusual header text, so this RFC puts non-ASCII header text into a shape those programs will pass through untouched, and tells newer programs how to unpack it again.

sections.title: The Syntax of an Encoded-Word
sections.content:
An encoded-word is defined by an ABNF grammar, with the notation of RFC 822, except that whitespace characters may not appear between the components of an encoded-word: encoded-word = "=?" charset "?" encoding "?" encoded-text "?=". The charset and the encoding are tokens, and the encoded-text is one or more printable ASCII characters other than ? or SPACE.

Both the encoding and the charset names are case-independent, so the charset name ISO-8859-1 is equivalent to iso-8859-1, and the encoding named Q may be spelled either way.

An encoded-word may not be more than 75 characters long, including charset, encoding, encoded-text and delimiters. If it is desirable to encode more text than will fit in one encoded-word, multiple encoded-words separated by CRLF SPACE may be used. While there is no limit to the length of a multiple-line header field, each line of a header field that contains one or more encoded-words is limited to 76 characters. The length restrictions are there to ease interoperability through internetwork mail gateways and to limit how far ahead a header parser must look for the final ?= delimiter before it can decide whether what it has is an encoded-word or ordinary text.
sections.plainLanguage: An encoded-word starts with the characters =? and ends with ?=, with a character set name and an encoding name in between and the text itself last. It must be no more than 75 characters long, and a longer piece of text is split across several encoded-words.

sections.title: The B and Q Encodings
sections.content:
The charset portion of an encoded-word specifies the character set associated with the unencoded text. It can be any of the character set names allowed in an RFC 1521 charset parameter of a text/plain body part, or any character set name registered with IANA for use with the MIME text/plain content type. Some character sets use code-switching techniques to switch between ASCII mode and other modes; if unencoded text in an encoded-word contains control codes to switch out of ASCII mode, it must also contain additional control codes so that ASCII mode is selected again at the end of the encoded-word.

When there is a possibility of using more than one character set and there are no private agreements between sender and recipients, the RFC recommends that members of the ISO-8859-* series be used in preference to other character sets.

The initial legal values for the encoding are Q and B. The Q encoding is recommended when most of the characters to be encoded are in the ASCII character set; otherwise the B encoding should be used. A mail reader which claims to recognise encoded-words MUST be able to accept either encoding for any character set it supports. The B encoding is identical to the BASE64 encoding defined by RFC 1521. The Q encoding is similar to the Quoted-Printable content-transfer-encoding: any 8-bit value may be represented by = followed by two hexadecimal digits, the 8-bit value 20 may be written as an underscore, and 8-bit values for printable ASCII characters other than =, ?, underscore and SPACE may be written as themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: Two ways of writing the text are defined. The B way is the same base64 coding used for message bodies. The Q way is like quoted-printable, so text that is mostly plain English stays readable, with only the unusual characters written as an equals sign and two hexadecimal digits.

sections.title: Where an Encoded-Word May Appear
sections.content:
An encoded-word may replace a text token in any Subject or Comments header field, any extension message header field, or any RFC 1521 body part field for which the field body is defined as *text. It may also appear in any user-defined X- message or body part header field. Ordinary ASCII text and encoded-words may appear together in the same header field, but an encoded-word in a field defined as *text MUST be separated from any adjacent encoded-word or text by linear-white-space.

An encoded-word may appear within a comment delimited by parentheses, wherever a comment character is allowed. Within a phrase, for example one that precedes an address in a From, To or Cc header, an encoded-word may replace a word entity, and the set of characters that may be used in a Q-encoded encoded-word there is restricted to upper and lower case ASCII letters, decimal digits, and the punctuation characters exclamation mark, asterisk, plus sign, hyphen, slash, equals sign and underscore.

These are the only locations where an encoded-word may appear. An encoded-word MUST NOT appear in any portion of an addr-spec, and it MUST NOT be used in a Received header field. Each encoded-word MUST encode an integral number of octets, the encoded-text may not be continued in the next encoded-word, and each encoded-word MUST represent an integral number of characters, so a multi-octet character may not be split across adjacent encoded-words.
sections.plainLanguage: Encoded text is allowed in subject lines, comments, extension fields and the display name before an address. It is not allowed inside an address itself, and not in the Received header that records where a message came from.

sections.title: Recognising and Displaying Encoded-Words
sections.content:
When a mail reader parses the message and body part headers according to the rules in RFC 822, it recognises encoded-words as follows. In a field defined as *text, or any user-defined header field, each sequence of up to 75 printable characters that contains no linear-white-space should be examined to see if it is an encoded-word according to the syntax rules, and any other sequence should be treated as ordinary ASCII text. In a field not defined as *text, the field is parsed according to its own syntax rules, but any word that appears within a phrase should be treated as an encoded-word if it meets the syntax rules. Within a comment, any sequence of up to 75 printable characters that meets the syntax rules should be treated as an encoded-word.

Recognised encoded-words are decoded, and if possible the resulting unencoded text is displayed in the original character set. When a header field contains several encoded-words, any whitespace separating a pair of adjacent encoded-words is ignored. A mail reader need not attempt to display the text of an encoded-word that is incorrectly formed, but it MUST NOT prevent the display or handling of a message because an encoded-word is incorrectly formed.

The Conformance section says a mail composing program claiming compliance MUST ensure that any string of non-white-space printable ASCII characters within a *text or *ctext that begins with =? and ends with ?= is a valid encoded-word, and that any word within a phrase that begins and ends that way must be a valid encoded-word. A mail reading program claiming compliance must support both the B and Q encodings for any character set it supports.
sections.plainLanguage: A reader scans the header for short runs of ordinary printable characters and checks whether each one has the shape of an encoded-word. If it does, the reader decodes it and shows the original text. A broken encoded-word must not stop the message from being shown at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The Security Considerations section of the memo says that security issues are not discussed in it. The memo is concerned only with the syntax of header fields and with how mail programs should recognise, decode and display them. It notes along the way that because the encoding schemes allow arbitrary octet values to be encoded, mail readers that implement the decoding should ensure that displaying the decoded data on the recipient's terminal will not cause unwanted side effects.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo says nothing about security. It only defines how header text is written and read, and it warns that a reader should be careful about what it prints.

viz.caption: THE ENCODED-WORD GRAMMAR FROM RFC 1522, SECTION 2

data.title: An encoded-word
data.code:
encoded-word = "=?" charset "?" encoding "?" encoded-text "?="

charset = token
encoding = token

token = 1*<Any CHAR except SPACE, CTLs, and especials>

especials = "(" / ")" / "<" / ">" / "@" / "," / ";" / ":" /
           "\"" / "/" / "[" / "]" / "?" / "." / "="

encoded-text = 1*<Any printable ASCII character other
                 than "?" or SPACE>

viz.caption: THE TWO ENCODINGS DEFINED BY RFC 1522

cells: Identical to the BASE64 encoding defined by RFC 1521.
Like the Quoted-Printable content-transfer-encoding: an equals sign and two hexadecimal digits for any 8-bit value, an underscore for the space, and printable ASCII kept as itself.
